result:
Solution 3 gives the answer I believe is correct, but I am relying partly on recall of the literature rather than a full derivation.

**Solution 1 (q ≈ 2.6067).** The "Erdős–Borwein" ladder of exponents 1/3, 1/7, 1/15, … is asserted without a real derivation. The recursions it cites look constructed to produce that constant. I don't trust this value.

**Solution 2 (q = 1 + ln 2).** The integral ∫ dg / (g(g−1)) over g from 2 to ∞ is evaluated correctly, but the claim that it measures the optimal architecture is unjustified. The step from nested combs to a trial exponent is heuristic and looks tuned to give ln 2. I don't trust this value either.

**Solution 3 (q = 2).** The mechanism is a mass-transport argument. A pile of mass M at distance d reaches the origin only if M exceeds roughly (1−μ) times the ball volume. Summing over the sphere, the sphere size cancels, leaving E[u(o)] ≲ Σ_d V(d)^{1−p}. Since V(d) ≥ d on any infinite connected graph, this sum is finite for p > 2. That gives a plausible upper bound: stabilization for p > 2 on every bounded-degree graph.

The lower-bound argument is weaker. On ℤ, an infinite expected odometer for p ≤ 2 does not by itself imply explosion, because the odometer can be infinite in expectation while still finite almost surely. In fact ℤ should stabilize with only a finite mean, since Σ_d P(M > cd) converges. A matching explosion for p < 2 therefore needs more elaborate graphs, not ℤ itself. The combs in Solutions 1 and 2 only push the threshold above 4/3, so they don't contradict q = 2. The value q = 2 also agrees with my recollection of the sharp moment threshold for this model.

The final value in Solution 3 matches what I believe is the true answer, even though its sharpness argument is flawed.

CHOICE: 3
